quote: Early studiers of cults were surprised to discover than when cults receive a major shock—a prophecy fails to come true, a moral flaw of the founder is revealed—they often come back stronger than before
content: This is the folklore of one book, and the book's own case did not behave as described. Festinger's Seekers dissolved within months of the failed landing; the group had been infiltrated by observers who made up a noticeable share of its active membership, a fact later critics regarded as having propped it up. The first attempt to replicate the increased-proselytizing finding, with a Pentecostal group whose prophesied nuclear attack did not occur, found no increase (Hardyck & Braden 1962), and the subsequent literature finds that the typical responses to failed prophecy are reinterpretation, quiet decline and schism, with increased fervor the exception. The Jehovah's Witnesses example fails too: the Watchtower never officially placed Armageddon in 1975, and after 1975 the organization suffered the only sustained membership decline in its history. The essay opens by describing as an established surprise a pattern that the field, on examination, did not find.

quote: For that matter, I can’t recall seeing the evaporative cooling analogy elsewhere, though that doesn’t mean it hasn’t been noted before.
content: It had been, in a book that is standard in three disciplines. Hirschman's Exit, Voice, and Loyalty (1970, book, no DOI) sets out exactly this dynamic: when an organization deteriorates, its most quality-sensitive members are the first to exit, their exit removes the voices most able to correct the deterioration, and the organization worsens further. Hirschman's prescription is also the essay's, that organizations should raise the cost of exit or lower the cost of voice to keep the critics inside. The mechanism is real, the essay's application to cults and mailing lists is apt, and the Objectivist example is consistent with it. The annotation is only that a reader who wants the theory with its evidence and its qualifications, including the conditions under which exit improves rather than degrades the remainder, should read the thirty-seven-year-old original rather than the Java applet.
